item.title: How Australia combines modern tech and Indigenous knowledge to fight fire
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czdmvr984yyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
How Australia combines modern tech and Indigenous knowledge to fight fire - Published The wildfires currently ravaging Europe feel close to home for Professor Marta Yebra, despite being on the other side of the world. Originally from Spain, the Canberra-based bushfire expert has spent years developing ways for Australia - home to some of the most fire-prone landscapes in the world - to battle its own blazes. She heads up the Bushfire Research Centre of Excellence, which was set up in the aftermath of Australia's worst fire season on record: the Black Summer fires of 2019-20, which razed a combined area about the size of the UK. Her team looks at how technology such as satellites, drones and AI can be used to better detect fires, alongside the knowledge of experienced firefighters. Equally important, though, is the knowledge and experience that has accrued in Australia over thousands of years, and has been passed down through generations. This is where Australia has an advantage. The use of fire has been part of the country's Indigenous culture since long before Europeans arrived in the 18th century - but the value of this ingrained knowledge has only been truly realised in recent years. From outer space to underground Yebra has spearheaded an innovative project, bringing together millennia-old knowledge in Australia's Indigenous communities with cutting-edge satellite imagery to help detect where fires are most likely to break out. The satellite images pick up the "fuel moisture content" in the landscape, which signals where there might be a large amount of fuel, such as dry leaves, grass, shrubs and bark. But such data provides just one part of a bigger picture. That's where the likes of Adrian Webster come in. Growing up on the south coast of New South Wales (NSW), Webster learnt how to read the environment or "country" - the term Indigenous Australians use for their ancestral homeland – from his elders. Using Indigenous ecological knowledge – a plant's colour and scent, for example, or the shade cover of trees - he can verify information in the satellite images from Yebra's team. "She had all this amazing data, but there was no translation to what it meant on the ground, so it was kind of useless," he explains. "But through an Indigenous perspective, it was not useless. It was a map that could guide you through the country and, if you understood it, take you directly into a place that is ready to burn." For Webster, assessing the land involves him "literally digging and going underground," he says. "We're looking at the subsurface level and then everything from that up beyond the canopy." Yebra said there was a "remarkable agreement" between Webster's local knowledge and the satellite data, demonstrating the combined value of Indigenous expertise and Western science. Her team now hopes to get more funding for the project, and work with Indigenous communities to co-design plans to protect the land and manage fires. For Webster, it's about "allowing our mother – the planet Earth – a voice again". Fire as friend, not just foe Another example of ancient wisdom influencing modern techniques can be found in the way Australia fights fire with fire. Cultural burning refers to a longstanding practice by Indigenous Australians to manage the environment while also maintaining a deep, spiritual connection to the land. Part of it is lighting "cool fires": small, controlled blazes that create a patchy landscape, so fuel does not build up in one area. "In Europe, there is no such cultural aspect to this kind of landscape planning," Yebra says. Wildfire scientists in Spain have blamed a massive build-up of fuel for the blazes currently devastating the country. "It is difficult to watch what is happening in Spain, but it is not surprising," Yebra says. "Particularly as climate change is increasing the frequency of extreme fire weather across southern Europe." She believes Europe, facing its worst wildfires in decades, could benefit from Australia's firefighting experience. "We have decades of experience living with large and high-intensity bushfires," she says. "One of the biggest changes we are seeing in bushfire management is a shift from simply reacting to fires towards anticipating risk and acting earlier. "The earlier we can identify risk or detect an ignition, the more options firefighters have." Webster says a key lesson the world could learn from Australia is "don't sit back and wait". "The longer you leave it, the more fuel there is to burn, so the fire is naturally going to be bigger and harder to extinguish," he says. "Indigenous people always knew that, so we burnt continuously all the time. That way there was no fuel for big fires." The practice of lighting cool fires dates back 60,000 years. Part of Webster's role is to assess the area before one is lit, looking for natural signs of oil and water in the landscape so that the blaze remains under control. "All the answers are in the environment," he says. "There's a sweet spot in the middle where there's enough water to slow that fire down but there's enough oil to push that fire on." A more modern tactic used across Australia is a prescribed burn, also known as a hazard reduction burn. These carefully planned, often large-scale fires are usually carried out during cooler months, and are increasingly being adopted in parts of Europe. It's an approach that has become especially vital in the "urban fringes", says superintendent Andrew Shurety from Fire and Rescue NSW. As Australia's population grows and suburbs expand, more people are moving closer to bushland, making hazard burns firefighters' "main mitigating factor that we try to do to reduce the risk of bushfires because we know they're going to come". The problem, Shurety points out, is that longer fire seasons and more rain during cooler months shortens the window that such burns can be carried out. Starving a fire of fuel is also the idea behind "backburning", a widely accepted practice in Australia where a blaze is deliberately lit ahead of a main fire to strip out the vegetation and try to stop it from spreading. This approach is also being increasingly adopted overseas - as Queensland firefighter Damian Hatfield found out. When he travelled to Alberta, Canada with a contingent of Australian firefighters to help tackle the country's worst wildfires on record, backburning was not widely used. A year later, things had shifted. "Backburning was definitely much more at the forefront when I returned in 2024," he says, with Canadian firefighters showing "no hesitation" to include the approach in their operations. Drones have also transformed how Australia deals with bushfires, says Trent Curtin, from the Rural Fire Service in NSW - particularly in recent years. "The local crews arrive, send a drone up quickly, have a look at where the fire is and how it's progressing, get some intelligence and make decisions before we can even get our large helicopters or other aircraft down," Curtin explains. Drones also deliver heavy gear to crews on the ground, start blazes for backburning operations and help assess the damage caused by fires. The summer ahead Back at Yebra's centre, the team's work is particularly timely with weather forecasters predicting a super El Nino this summer - which could increase the probability of extreme heat, drought and bushfires. "Our next fire season is looking like it's going to be a bad one," Yebra says. That concern is shared by Jason Heffernan, chief officer of the Country Fire Authority in Australia's southeastern state of Victoria. Here, the memories of 2009's Black Saturday bushfires – the country's deadliest on record – loom large. "For this summer coming, we're bracing for what could be something extremely significant," Heffernan says. Even in the broader scheme of things, he notes that local fire seasons are starting earlier and lasting longer. "Unfortunately for Australia", he adds, "our environment is designed to burn." But as the world braces for wildfires that are more frequent and intense, Heffernan also believes "we must take a global perspective". "No fire service can do this on their own and the key is to have formal and trusted networks," he says - as well as national and international resource-sharing arrangements. One of the challenges as a fire chief, he explains, is knowing when to ask for help - too late and the benefits will be lost, but too early and resources might be wasted. Such a call was made just earlier this week, when France sent its first-ever request for help from Australian firefighters. Two dozen crew and several aircraft will be deployed as France battles record-breaking wildfires amid a prolonged summer heatwave. Australia regularly sends specialist teams to the US and Canada, and vice versa, with many requests for what's known as "arduous fire crews": those who have fought fires in rugged and remote areas. There are far fewer requests from Europe, Heffernan says - but this may change as "the global fire community is becoming more connected". As he points out, while forests and climates vary across the globe, "we're seeing bushfires occur in parts of the world that never had bushfires before". - Published8 hours ago - Published11 June

item.title: Solitude as a new aspirational lifestyle: 'We are not lonely'
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y63dw2x3wo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Solitude as a new aspirational lifestyle: 'We are not lonely' - Published It's a Friday night. A young woman trudges back to her apartment after a day of work. She enters a spotless kitchen, unloads a bag of groceries, and unwraps a frozen pizza before sliding it in the oven. What follows is a nightly routine that is almost meditative in its mundanity: she lights a candle and gazes briefly at the snow-covered landscape outside her window, piles a premade salad onto a plate with the pizza, and settles on her sofa to eat in front of the TV. The tagline that accompanies the scene reads: "POV you're a childfree and single girl that has no friends and lives alone so this is how you spend your Friday night." At the centre of the video – which has amassed seven million views on TikTok – is Lana Isa, a software sales manager in her 20s based in Toronto. In addition to chronicling her nightly self-care routines, she takes her almost 400,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram on late-night fast food drives, reading sessions perched on a rock by the lake, even a saga of getting locked out of her apartment in the middle of the night. Isa is part of a growing, albeit niche corner of the internet where content creators, many of them women, share their daily rituals of living alone, choosing to spotlight a lifestyle that prioritises peace and solitude - the antithesis of social media excess. For Isa, unveiling the "no friends" aspect of her life was less of a tagline, but the "reality" she had been living for several years. Alone, but not lonely After switching several high schools, enduring Covid isolation during her college years and moving across the country following her first heartbreak, Isa found herself forced to adjust to living alone with no close friends. "People don't talk about having no friends a lot... I think it's still what people would consider embarrassing or a little taboo," she says. When she started sharing the friendlessness of her circumstances on social media, an audience began to connect. Her initial following of around 2,000 followers on TikTok swelled to more than 175,000 in the span of eight months. "It was eye-opening to see other people who are living the same situation that I've been… and to feel like I could kind of relate to people for the first time in a while." And relate they did. Isa's comments section filled with people bonding over similar experiences of living alone or having no friends, and finding comfort in "feeling seen". As with most trends online, curiosity quickly turned to backlash. Isa and similar creators were dubbed "loneliness influencers", with some framing them as part of a new demographic of sad, lonely, childless women in crisis. Others accused them of romanticising self isolation and encouraging an "air of cosy defeatism" by shunning social connections. But their reels paint a lifestyle that may be more relatable than many would care to admit. These women take themselves on solo dates, embark on spontaneous road trips, and even push through the awkwardness of attending parties alone. Destigmatising loneliness For Devon Noehring, a full-time content creator and self-proclaimed introvert based in Phoenix, Arizona, it's been "frustrating" to see her solo weekends cooking and lounging at home with her dog reduced to a symptom of female loneliness. "It's the exact opposite intention of our videos," she says. "I just hate the stigma of alone equalling lonely." While Noehring does have a close group of friends, growing up she always felt "ashamed" of being the quiet girl with social anxiety. It wasn't until she confessed her insecurities online that she discovered a following of fellow introverts who identified with her struggles. "Being alone is where I feel my most free and most like myself," she says. "That's how I recharge, and I feel very proud of myself for being independent and doing things alone… I think it's something that should be celebrated." Some health researchers have been working to "destigmatise loneliness" by differentiating between chronic loneliness forced by circumstance and those who have agency to choose to live and spend time alone. "Everybody's lonely at some point, but some people are not OK admitting that," says Professor Melody Ding, an epidemiologist researching social connection and loneliness at the University of Sydney. "That can create this false expectation that you have to be socially happy and connected all the time." But she cautions that while influencers can make being alone look "really appealing", humans still need social connection and it can be detrimental to one's mental and physical wellbeing to be stuck in a cycle of intense isolation. "We're a social species," says Ding. "We survive better with companionship, with people around us." She acknowledges that people's social needs vary at different stages of life, but Ding's hope for those who have lost relationships is that they can eventually "de-emphasise" the friendless aspect of their lives and forge new social bonds. "It's important we have people in our life and it's important these relationships are positive and nourish our lives," Ding adds. 'We want to find people we relate to' Even in moments when they do feel lonely, these women say loneliness doesn't define their lives, nor do they aspire to remain permanently friendless. "We never describe ourselves as lonely," says SJ Hoadley, who works as a cleaner in the UK and began documenting her own solo living after discovering Isa's videos. "I think sometimes my lack of friends tends to bother the people around me more than it bothers me." After leaving a seven-year abusive relationship, she moved to a new area where she knew no one and was confronted with having to rebuild her life. Despite the initial "shock", she eventually started "enjoying and embracing that independence" and "getting to feel comfortable with my own company". In a social media ecosystem that thrives on flooding our feeds with aspirational living and a perennial state of FOMO (fear of missing out), the rise of solo living influencers can be validating for those who see themselves reflected in the lifestyle, says Dr Anne Oeldorf-Hirsch at the University of Connecticut who specialises in how humans build community online. "There's been this kind of long growing backlash against the idea that we're seeing everybody's perfect life, their highlight reel," she says. Oeldorf-Hirsch believes the appeal of solitude content is filling a social need for the creators and their audience, providing some "balance" against the dominance of hyper-glamourised influencer culture. "We're kind of trending towards these influencers that are more authentic, living their true life," she says. "We just want to find people we relate to." Hoadley has seen her following surge at times by tens of thousands per day, while Noehring's videos have garnered millions of views across her channels. Those online connections have made Hoadley excited for a future where she finds a "little group of girlfriends". Noehring hopes to one day organise a real world meet-up with her virtual community, and Isa says the support has given her the "push" she needed to start thinking about making friends again. "I think that what all the content is saying is: find your path," says Hoadley. "It doesn't have to be this one-size-fits-all that we keep getting pushed on social media."

item.title: Ginger hair portraits show unexpected 'golden thread' connecting Americans
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce97nyz4rvmo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Ginger hair portraits show unexpected 'golden thread' connecting Americans - Published For Kieran Dodds, photographing people with red hair has become something of an obsession over the past decade. The 45-year-old, from Edinburgh, who is himself a "proud ginger", began taking pictures in his homeland in 2013 as part of a series examining Scottish identity. His interest in the subject soon took him to other ginger hotspots such the Russian city of Perm and Jamaica's Treasure Beach. His 2020 book Gingers spanned the world but after its release he notice there was a "huge gap". "I realised I didn't have any American citizens," Kieran told the BBC. "Then all these people got in touch." "I was like 'oh wow, of course, the whole world is in the States'," Kieran says. "It's a microcosm." He says a message from a Native American man who had red hair instantly aroused his curiosity. "I found it very interesting and it made me think, 'where on earth did it come from?'" The cover of his latest book - Gingers of America, external - features Joshua Elliot from the Muscogee (Creek) Nation in Oklahoma. He told Kieran that some of his mother's relatives were German and on his dad's side there were people from England and Sweden, so that could explain where his ginger hair comes from. "My mom's side has always been involved with the Muscogee tribe and traditions and I've grown up around it," he said. Joshua knows he does not fit people's expectations of what a Native American should look like, but he said: "Our chief's wife told me it's about your involvement in your community and your tribe, the people around you and what you put back into it. "Which I really took to heart." Kieran spoke to a lot of Native Americans on his visits and most knew of a European ancestry which could explain their red hair. "The thing that surprised me was how early on there were these Scots and Irish marrying Native Americans," he said. Lottie Wahkinney, a Comanche girl from Oklahoma, has Scottish grandparents, from Galashiels. Her father Jared told Kieran his dad was Comanche but his mum was born and raised in Scotland. "That's why my Lottie has a good mix of everything going on," Jared said. "My Scottish grandparents would come over every summer. "On my first visit to Scotland when I was 22, folks were like, 'Where are your moccasins? Where's your headdress?'. "I explained 'I wear Nikes'." While most Native Americans could explain where the ginger gene might have come from, there was one exception - a Cherokee girl called Lakia - whose family knew of no European ancestry. "It is a totally different colour of red," Kieran said. "It's deep ruby. That really intrigued me." In the book, Lakia says that all her family, on both sides, have jet-black straight hair but hers turned red during her childhood. "Everyone thought, since I was about eight, that I dyed my hair," she said. "And still now everyone's like, 'what hair colour is that?'." After meeting Native Americans, Kieran knew there was something in the US he could explore. Over the next few years, he made seven lengthy trips, often linked to his full-time profession as an environmental photographer. One state he found surprising was Alabama, a place many in the UK associate with racial segregation and the struggle for civil rights as well as its pioneering space exploration programmes. "I knew it for racism and Nasa," Kieran said. "In my head it was stuck in the 60s but Birmingham is an incredibly vibrant city. "I met a lot of black Americans who had often married someone who is white." Rachel Releford told Kieran that when she goes out with her daughter Liliana people think she is the nanny or the babysitter. "I'm like, 'nope, she's mine'," Rachel said. "I think you still get some people who grew up with the mindset that things need to be segregated. "Some of my grandparents' friends were a little hesitant when they found out I was dating my husband. They said: 'You're really going to let her date someone of a different race?' "But my grandparents were like, 'Go for it. He's a cool guy, he's a sweet one.' I love him for who he is. He's a great human being." Also in Alabama, he met Henry Davis and his young son Henry Davis II. The older man no longer has any red hair but he says he looked just like his son when he was the same age. "We're not really sure where it comes from," Henry senior said. "My dad is turning grey now. He'll get some red in his beard, and then it kind of goes grey. "So I guess it's from his side." As someone who grew up with red hair himself, Kieran says he is well aware that ginger can be used as an insult. However, he says: "I use the word for its descriptive power because red is the colour of fire engines and blood whereas ginger has a golden tone to it. "You can use it in a kind way." He says the book uses ginger hair as "a golden thread" that weaves together America's diverse and difficult history in a way which shows a connection between people. "That's my big idea," Kieran says. "We are all made of the same stuff and with the ginger hair it shows." According to Kieran no-one exemplifies this better than a young lad named Cali whom he met in Alabama. "His background is everything - European, African-American, Hispanic and indigenous as well," he says. "His gran is white but was she unable to get married to a black guy in Alabama - even after the courts had made it legal. "She moved to Georgia and had a family there. It's an incredibly diverse family." In Scotland, it is thought as many as 13% of the population - about 700,000 people - are natural redheads, a higher percentage than anywhere else in the world. Globally, less than 2% of the population are thought to have red hair but Kieran's research lead him to believe the US figure is higher than that. "We landed on about 4% for the genetic prevalence," he says. "If all the gingers in America were gathered in one place, Gingertown would be about 14 million people. "It's a big city. You would see it from space it would be so bright." Kieran says the big difference between America and other places is that they tend to have really thought about where they come from. "Everyone has self-consciously moved from somewhere," he says. "And that includes the Native Americans, who have been moved from other parts of America. "That's what makes it interesting." He says his book is a road trip through the US trying to find out about the country through this unique trait. For Kieran, the recent men's football World Cup got people excited about the US again in a way they haven't been over the past few years because of political divisions. He says he was pleased to see people visiting the US and saying "it is not what I expected". "There's such a lot of amazing people and communities there," he says. "People you might connect with and agree with on a lot of things. "I'm quite heartened that the football has revealed that. "I feel quite patriotic for America now."

item.title: Death row inmates desperate to escape execution in Saudi Arabia call the BBC
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c80nkgdnl4no?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Death row inmates desperate to escape execution in Saudi Arabia call the BBC - Published There was desperation in the voice of the young Ethiopian man when he managed to get through to the BBC from a phone in his prison cell on death row in Saudi Arabia. Habtom, whose name - like the other prisoner featured in this article - has been changed to protect his identity, has been held in a jail in the southern city of Khamis Mushait for more than three years. Above the noise of cellmates shouting behind him, he pleaded for help and sounded angry that his government appeared to be doing little to change his fate. "One prisoner cannot comfort another. We have no choice but to cry. We are waiting for our turn, even though we do not know when it will happen," said Habtom. He and some of his fellow inmates had fled war and poverty at home in the hope of finding a better life. But that quest, which took him through Djibouti and Yemen, led to his incarceration - joining a growing number of Ethiopians in Saudi prisons who face the prospect of execution for drug-smuggling offences. Anxious to tell their story, some of the prisoners managed to get hold of the mobile phone number for the BBC's Tigrinya language service. In total we have spoken to seven of the dozens - perhaps as many as 200 - Ethiopians inside the prison who are waiting for a death sentence to be carried out. Other foreigners, including Pakistanis, Sudanese and Jordanians, are in a similar position, but in the first seven months of this year 17 Ethiopians have been executed - the highest number among non-Saudis. Five of those executions happened on Monday. Two years ago, according to research by Amnesty International, just two Ethiopians were executed, but 35 were put to death in 2025. It is not clear exactly why there has been an uptick, but it could be linked to more people leaving the northern Ethiopian region of Tigray, where a brutal two-year civil war in Tigray ended in late 2022, leaving devastation in its wake. "It may also be linked to Saudi Arabia's expanding use of the death penalty for drug-related offences in recent years," Amnesty International researcher Dana Ahmed tells the BBC. Habtom, who like most of those the BBC spoke to is from Tigray, was found guilty of smuggling hashish, a type of cannabis. In Saudi Arabia, on the judge's discretion, a guilty verdict can result in a death sentence. But rights groups - including Reprieve, Human Rights Watch (HRW) and Amnesty International - have said that in these kinds of cases due process is rarely followed. Defendants are not given access to a lawyer or the court papers - while translation, when it is offered, can be inadequate, Amnesty's Ahmed says. Although there is the theoretical right to appeal, without a lawyer they cannot submit one "and then the sentence is automatically upheld", she says. "There is a near-total lack of transparency throughout the entire judicial process, from sentencing to Supreme Court review and ratification by the King. People on death row and their families are left in the dark about their fate." Habtom alleged that he was not given the chance to speak to a lawyer or defend himself. He also said he was forced to sign a document in Arabic, which said he agreed to the sentence, without understanding what he was putting his name to. Other prisoners that the BBC spoke to had similar stories about the legal system. HRW has also contacted people close to the cases and learned about "mass sentences, mass trials that lacked any kind of due process and people detained then just waiting with no idea when the sentence would happen", Nadia Hardman, the organisation's senior adviser on refugee and migrant rights, said. The Saudi authorities did not respond to a BBC request for comment on allegations that the legal process was not fair, but every execution is accompanied by a statement issued through the official press agency. It outlines a clear process: an investigation, a court case, an appeal, a Supreme Court ruling and then a royal decree. The sentence reflects the commitment to protect citizens "from the scourge of drugs" and the damage they can cause, the statement adds. Habtom said that although he manged to keep in occasional contact with his family via the wall-mounted phone in his prison cell, he refused to tell them he was on death row: "I would rather they be told after I die than now." He had dreamt of finishing high school, graduating from college and getting a job to support his parents - but the Tigray war put paid to that. "My goal was destroyed, so I decided to emigrate," he said. After surviving the dangerous journey to Saudi Arabia in 2021, Habtom found low-paid work as a goatherder, but his employers offered him and others a chance to earn more money. They were asked to deliver a package but were stopped by police on the way and were found with the narcotic leaf known as khat - a natural stimulant that is widely used in the Horn of Africa. The official Saudi statements all refer to hashish smuggling but those the BBC spoke to talked about khat. "I did not know what we were carrying. But later I was told it was khat. I don't even know what khat is," Habtom said, admitting that he was tempted into the work by the sum of money on offer. Habtom acknowledged he had "made a mistake without knowing it" and hoped that his sentence could be commuted to prison time. Three of his fellow Ethiopian detainees were executed in April - another nine were killed in June. The April killings sparked an outcry from rights groups and some leading Ethiopian figures, including the influential head of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. Patriarch Abune Mathias urged the government to negotiate with the Saudi authorities and called the inmates "voiceless children" living "under the shadow of death". In its April report, HRW called on the Saudi authorities to immediately halt executions of Ethiopian migrants and ensure all cases were handled in line with international law. It also asked Ethiopia's foreign ministry to intervene urgently and provide consular support. The safety of Ethiopians in general in Saudi Arabia was raised at a meeting in Addis Ababa in May between Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos and Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister Waleed Al-Khuraiji. This was followed in June by a visit to the prison by Ethiopia's Ambassador Tafa Tulu Dadi, though the prisoners told the BBC that they were not given enough time to explain their situation to him. It also appeared to have limited impact as in the following week more Ethiopians were executed. The African Union's human rights commission has also urged Ethiopia to safeguard the lives of Ethiopians facing execution in Saudi Arabia. The BBC has contacted Ethiopian officials in Saudi Arabia and the government in Addis Ababa for comment but has not received a response. Without referring to the death penalty specifically, Ethiopia's foreign ministry did release a statement on 13 July saying it was in regular contact with the Saudi authorities "pursuing appropriate remedies for Ethiopian citizens facing difficult circumstances". It added that "to date" nearly 2,000 Ethiopians had "benefited from royal amnesties" - without mentioning the crimes or sentences. As they await the outcome of diplomatic manoeuvres, the prisoners who spoke to the BBC said they were enduring hardships in overcrowded facilities. Desta, located in another part of the prison, said there were 200 men in his cell crammed into an area designed for 90 people, with 45 bunk beds arranged around the walls. During the day, the prisoners sat on the floor in stifling conditions squeezed up next to one another; when the temperature dropped at night, they covered themselves with rubbish bags in lieu of bed sheets, he said. "The stress of facing execution, combined with the overcrowded conditions, exposes us to illness and anxiety," Desta said. "The guard only opens the door to bring food, covering his mouth and nose with a mask - that is the only time the door is opened. After he gives us the food, he quickly locks it and leaves. "It is not possible to ask them any questions or speak to them. Even if you ask, there is severe beating." He was arrested while trying to cross the border from Yemen more than three years ago and accused of smuggling drugs. "We were four Ethiopians, and there was one Yemeni with us. He told us he could help us cross the border safely because he knew the safest route. In return, he asked us to carry packages containing khat and even promised to pay us some money. "Unfortunately, shortly after we crossed, we were captured by police officers. They opened fire on us, and the Yemeni man ran away, but we couldn't. We were shocked and had no idea where to go." Like all those interviewed by the BBC, Desta said he had never expected to be sentenced to death and believed he would eventually return home after serving time in prison. Instead, he alleged that he was also forced to sign a document in Arabic that listed charges carrying capital punishment. Later, when he appeared in court, he said that he was denied the chance to challenge the charges and had no legal representation. "When you appear before the judge on the first day, he asks: 'Do you accept the charges?' On the second appearance, he sentences you to death," Desta said. As a brick-maker struggling to support his family, he had left Tigray during the war as the fighting edged closer to his home. Now he worries for his life again - and he, Habtom and dozens of others on death row are begging for outside help. "We are living in deep fear and cannot even eat the food we are given," said Habtom. item.title: Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/c998m4ve0rpo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes? - Published Life moves fast for Fifa president Gianni Infantino. It was doing so last month as he was zig-zagging across the United States in a private jet to make him virtually omnipresent as the World Cup reached its crescendo. On 19 July he must have felt on top of the world as, together with US President Donald Trump, they handed the trophy over to Spain. Less than two weeks later, Infantino is in a lonely place after scrapping controversial plans to sell off stakes in Fifa competitions to private investment. Condemned by UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, castigated by fans of the game he professes to want to protect. These can easily be deflected as hazards of the job. Less so the threatened boycott of Fifa competitions by European governing body Uefa, and its subsequent stunning statement in which it declared it had lost confidence in Infantino's leadership. Concacaf (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and the AFC (Asia) also - in their own ways - have offered withering assessments of how Fifa is being run under Infantino. "This issue extends far beyond a single proposal," said the AFC. "Rather, it has exposed fundamental weaknesses in Fifa's consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed." Sources say, in addition to rejecting Infantino's plan, the vast majority of the Concacaf members are either losing faith in the Fifa president's ability to govern the game, or have lost it altogether. On top of that, Carlos Cordeiro, special adviser to Infantino and appointed by Trump as senior adviser to the White House Task Force on the 2026 World Cup, has resigned. Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said in a statement to Associated Press that Fifa's own administration was "deceived" about the project. BBC Sport has approached Fifa for comment. It feels as though the walls are closing in on Infantino. But if this is the beginning of the end of his tenure, who takes over? - Uefa has 'lost confidence' in Fifa leadership - Published9 hours ago - Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment plan - Published20 hours ago Might Infantino really go? Firstly, it is wise to be realistic. Speaking to BBC Sport earlier this week, former Football Association chairman David Bernstein said of Infantino: "In a normal organisation, if he has to back down due to something of this magnitude he'd probably be shown the door. "But Fifa is not a normal organisation. If he has the support of enough of the national associations, he will continue." Former Fifa vice-president Jim Boyce said he thought Infantino would "still have enough support" to be re-elected but "if things continue at the pace they are continuing, who knows?" He added: "If I was a betting man, which I'm not, I would still bet he will get his final four-year term." Infantino has been Fifa president since 2016. Before that he was secretary general of Uefa for seven years. Few know the map of football politics better than him. Now 56, Infantino became president by beating Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88. His task was to clean up an organisation tainted by corruption allegations following the resignation of predecessor Sepp Blatter. Blatter was cleared of corruption charges last year. "I will work tirelessly to bring football back to Fifa and Fifa back to football," said Infantino at the time. He has twice been re-elected unopposed, and it was expected the same thing would happen again next March. This is not unusual. Blatter was unopposed in 2007 and 2011. Brazilian Joao Havelange was the last person to unseat a Fifa president in an election, ousting Sir Stanley Rous in 1974. No-one opposed Havelange for five straight terms until he finally resigned in 1998, aged 82. Letters of support backing Infantino's re-election have been submitted. Will they be withdrawn? Who might replace him? Victor Montagliani (Concacaf president) Like Infantino, he was elected in 2016 promising governance reform. A former president of Canada Soccer, Montagliani was heavily involved in the build up to, and delivery of the 2026 World Cup, the first to be hosted by three nations. He is fluent in French, Italian and Spanish, as well as English. Explaining his decision to run for the Concacaf presidency, Montagliani told the BC Business website: "Like anything, when I decide to go, I go. I campaigned on my own dime for three months, went to see all 41 countries, from the US to Bonaire, a little island off Venezuela." Montagliani took the lead when Concacaf hosted an expanded Copa America in 2024 - in an interview with BBC Sport he rejected the idea it could become a regular occurrence. Politically strong, he smoothed relations around Arsene Wenger's attempt to gain support for a World Cup every two years and has never truly bought into the idea of a 64-team World Cup. At the Leaders conference in 2025, he outlined why he felt football was strong enough to ride out any storm. "The game is bigger than world current leaders," he said. "Football will survive regimes. Does it cause a headache? Of course. You have to be realistic about that. That is the beauty of our game, it is bigger than any individual and country." Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa (AFC president) Initially elected in 2013, he was elected unopposed for a fourth term to run to 2027. The Bahraini has presided over significant growth within the Asian confederation, through the Champions League Elite, Champions League Two, the Challenge League and the Women's Champions League, which was launched in 2024-25. The Asian Cup has been expanded to 24 teams. Sheikh Salman signed off the brutal takedown of how Fifa is being run by Infantino and has carried with him a 46-member confederation, many of whom are aware the figures being offered by Infantino's plan are huge in terms of their overall football expenditure. Nasser Al-Khelaifi (PSG president and chair of European Football Clubs) Al-Khelaifi took over as chairman of the European Clubs' Association in the aftermath of the other seismic event that threatened to pull the game apart - the ill-fated European Super League, which collapsed within 48 hours in 2021. Al-Khelaifi presided over a name change - to European Football Clubs. More importantly, he expanded it to more than 800 members. Of the biggest clubs, only Real Madrid remain outside. In theory, the Qatari would be a serious challenger to Infantino. But it seems he doesn't want the role. "He genuinely, genuinely, genuinely doesn't want the job," was the response of a source close to the 52-year-old when asked about the possibility on Thursday. Mattias Grafstrom (Fifa secretary general) Appointed in May 2024 and an increasingly influential voice around the Fifa table. Multi-lingual Grafstrom become Infantino's chief of staff following his election as president in 2016. Another very visual presence at the World Cup, he could be seen as being too close to Infantino - and the general feeling Fifa's next president needs to be a non-European might also count against him. Fifa's next president will be confirmed at the organisation's 77th Congress in Morocco next March. Candidates have until 18 November to put their names forward. item.title: Bowen: Plan for Hamas to disarm faces big obstacles, yet it offers rare hope for Gaza
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2dkje4p4klo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Bowen: Plan for Hamas to disarm faces big obstacles, yet it offers rare hope for Gaza - Published There are many reasons why it might not work. At the same time, it is potentially a rare chink of light in a bleak picture. Hamas has never agreed to disarm before now. Handled carefully and well, there is a chance now to make diplomatic progress. A bargain lies at the heart of the new proposition for Hamas to disarm in Gaza. The idea is that as Hamas hands over its weapons, Israel pulls out of the 70% of Gaza that it occupies. That may sound simple, but the realities of politics, war, zero trust, the deaths of thousands and the destruction of Gaza make the process very complicated. Life in Gaza is catastrophic for well over 2 million Palestinian civilians who are living in desperate conditions. For most, Israel has destroyed their homes and their livelihoods. Israel killed more than 70,000 Palestinians during the war, and more than 1,000 more since the ceasefire, according to the Hamas-run health ministry whose figures are seen as reliable by the UN. Unicef says that Israel has killed more than 20,000 children since 7 October 2023, with at least 1,000 babies among the dead and wounded. Much of Gaza is rubble. It is not just the damage caused by Israel Defense Forces (IDF) military operations. There has also been an organised, officially sponsored project to destroy communities and smash infrastructure. Civilian demolition contractors from Israel have been contracted to finish the job started by IDF bombs. Many Palestinians believe Israel wants to force them out, by making life so insupportable and appalling that they will leave if they get the chance. Leaders and senior officials inside Jordan and Egypt also believe that powerful individuals in the Israeli government are working to create the conditions for the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians, most likely across their borders. On the Israeli side, there is a strong sense in the Jewish majority of 80% or so that Hamas will remain a potentially deadly threat until it is totally disarmed and stripped of any vestige of power. On 7 October 2023 Hamas and other Palestinians attacked Israel, killing almost 1,200 people, around two thirds of whom were civilians including children, and taking 251 people into Gaza as hostages. Many Israelis believe Hamas would do that again if it had the chance. The diplomatic process that produced the agreement with Hamas does not operate in a bubble. Making the plan work depends on broader issues too. Israel has a general election at the end of October. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is behind in the polls and fighting not just for his political life and legacy but potentially for his liberty. While he remains in office, his long running trial on corruption charges that could carry a jail sentence has been slowed to a crawl. That would change if he lost power. Netanyahu faces pressure at home and abroad. Domestically he does not want his political opponents to be able to accuse him of being soft on Hamas. Internationally the only address that matters to him is in Washington DC. The US also has elections looming with midterms in November. President Donald Trump cannot achieve a win in the war on Iran, so he needs one in Gaza. If Trump's Republican party loses badly, the power he relishes using will drain away. Trump will blame Netanyahu if he decides he is preventing the victory he wants and needs. One of Netanyahu's boasts to Israel's electorate is that he can handle the Americans, including Trump, better than any of his rivals. A Trump tirade before election day in Israel scuppers that proposition. Netanyahu is an expert at playing for time when faced with a big challenge. He will try to juggle pressure at home and pressure from the Oval Office until election day. Hamas is also under severe pressure. Most of its senior men and thousands of its fighters were killed by Israel. The IDF still assassinates senior Hamas figures when it gets a chance. As I write, a flash from the IDF on my phone says it has killed a commander of a Palestinian militia who it says took hostages on 7 October 2023. Many Palestinians blame Hamas for the consequences of its decision to attack Israel on 7 October. Hamas also faces challenges from powerful families and by militias funded and backed by Israel. It is trying to rebuild grass roots support. This was how the BBC's Gaza correspondent Rushdi Abu Alouf put it to me: "For months, Hamas increasingly shifted part of its focus back to social and political outreach, expanding Quran memorisation programmes and charitable activities aimed at children, teenagers and young people, while taking advantage of the severe humanitarian crisis and the growing dependence of so many families on aid." Khalil al Hayya, the newly confirmed political leader of Hamas, was a crucial player in the decision to drop objections to the framework. Egypt and Turkey did much of the hard diplomatic work to get him there. Hamas concessions are linked to Israel agreeing to pull back in Gaza. Israel is on record as demanding full Hamas disarmament as a pre-condition for withdrawal. - Bowen: Hamas diminished, but still part of the picture - Published1 day ago Only a step-by-step agreement, starting small and building confidence, has a chance of working. Trump will have to stay engaged, which is far from certain with a war with Iran among a planet full of other challenges. Just keeping the process going will require sustained diplomatic engagement and no sudden shocks that make meditation impossible. That will be difficult. The occupied West Bank is on the verge of an explosion of even worse violence. Figures gathered by ACLED, a group that monitors armed conflict, says that 2026 is on track to become the most violent year in the West Bank since it began monitoring the territory a decade ago. Jewish settlers have been allowed by the IDF and encouraged by extremists in the Netanyahu government to run riot, attacking and sometimes killing Palestinians and driving them off their land. Palestinians have been organising themselves to resist. Some opponents and critics of Netanyahu believe that he wants a major crisis on the West Bank to justify a tough response before the elections and remove any pressure to pull back in Gaza. Netanyahu and prominent ministers in his cabinet have said repeatedly that there will never be a Palestinian state. Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister, is committing the government to decisions aimed at increasing Jewish settlement and killing off the prospects of an independent Palestine. Smotrich is an extreme religious nationalist who has been sanctioned by major Western countries and banned from entering the UK, France, other leading European nations, as well as Australia and New Zealand. Israel condemned those decisions as antisemitic. A process that does not give Palestinians a political horizon and a route to self-determination will not work, condemning another generation to lives dominated by war. Diplomatic failure would not benefit Palestinians or Israelis. It would play into the hands of those on both sides who believe their conflict has no solution other than defeating their enemy. item.title: Police in the US are making their own true crime podcasts - will it help catch killers?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cpw9q0ekd9eo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Police in the US are making their own true crime podcasts - will it help catch killers? - Published Peter Chadwick had been on the run for nearly four years, charged with murdering his wife, when California police launched a podcast about the crime. He was captured in Mexico 10 months and 20 days later. Karen Schepers had been missing for more than four decades when another police force, in Illinois, debuted the first episode of a podcast last year about the cold case - and her body was found at the bottom of a river within weeks. Now Colorado investigators are hoping to bring in elusive tips about a 10-year-old unsolved murder, too. The Aurora Police Department (APD) released its own podcast this summer in an attempt to achieve justice for Chelsea Yasser, 21, who was found fatally stabbed in a shopping centre parking lot in 2016. As the barrelling behemoth of true crime content continues to flourish, police departments across the US and abroad are turning to podcast production for help solving cold murder cases and other investigations. "The true crime genre - whether it's TV, whether it's podcasts, whether it's books – I mean, it's wildly popular," says Joe Moylan, Aurora Police Department's public information officer. "And we absolutely were deliberate in trying to tap into that broader audience." The phenomenon is still in its infancy and brings its own benefits and pitfalls - but experts believe the trend will grow. "I think it's a tool that everyone will eventually embrace," says Michael Alcazar, retired NYPD detective and adjunct professor at John Jay College of Criminal Justice. True crime podcasts can air inaccurate information, he says, but this way police get to control what is out there and seek new tip-offs. There were already plenty of podcasts featuring former detectives discussing cases or policing issues, says Alyce McGovern, associate professor in criminology at University of New South Wales in Australia, where law enforcement has also begun dipping its toes into podcast production. But it's rarer for police department-produced podcasts to focus on cold cases and solicit tips, as the California, Colorado and Illinois departments have done. The police programmes are episodic in nature, outlining the crimes, victims and investigations with narrative panache and interesting details - much the same way that groundbreaking true crime podcast Serial did when it debuted in 2014. In Aurora, police hoped to produce a podcast that was equally engaging - and would prompt listeners to come forward with any relevant information. The killing of Chelsea Yasser has been described by the podcasters as the "White Whale", of Moby Dick fame, given how long it has haunted investigators. Yasser was fatally stabbed after getting into a minivan that pulled up in the parking lot; she collapsed moments after leaving the vehicle. Grainy surveillance footage captured the rocking van as the assault took place, but the images were not clear enough to discern a face and DNA recovered from under her fingernails matched no one in the system. As the APD released the podcast in June, detectives were testing the DNA using new forensic genealogy technology, and the programme updated listeners about other new lines of enquiry. The department has issued appeals for information on the Yasser murder before, but the podcast can cast a far wider net for witnesses and tipsters, Moylan says. "If you weren't watching the news that night when it happened, or if you didn't pick up a newspaper, you might not know anything about this case, so we wanted to tap into that broader audience. "Assuming that the suspect is still alive and out there somewhere, they could be anywhere in the country." The podcast had been downloaded 7,184 times by the end of July, according to APD - yielding several tips, including one which investigators continue to pursue. Most departments don't have the staff, budget or time needed to produce podcast content, nor do they have the equipment or expertise. Others hold off for fear of repercussions, lawsuits and civil liability, says retired detective Alcazar. In California, Newport Beach Police Department's podcast about the fugitive Chadwick, for example, was not without controversy. The millionaire was introduced to viewers in Episode 1 as "a man who killed his wife in the peaceful coastal community of Newport Beach, California in October 2012". Chadwick had been charged and pleaded not guilty, but not tried - yet the podcast made no use of the word "alleged" and called the millionaire a "murderer". Critics argued that it flew in the face of innocent-before-proven-guilty parameters and that the job of police was to investigate, not adjudicate. The podcast was produced and hosted by public information officer Jennifer Manzella, who defended the choice at the time, saying police "put out the same kinds of statements all the time". She tells BBC News that she was trying to balance telling the story in an engaging way without jeopardising the investigation. After Chadwick's August 2019 apprehension, he pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and was sentenced to 15 years to life in prison - where he remains. Manzella says it wasn't a direct tip from the podcast that led to his capture - but it undeniably helped because it put pressure on Chadwick while on the run, making him more likely to make mistakes. And investigators were able to obtain warrants and extraditions "in record time" because of the awareness - the podcast hit Number 24 on the iTunes chart. In the wake of the podcast - and Chadwick's capture - she got calls from other departments and agencies interested in producing something similar. But not everyone has been behind the idea. "I initially was not really interested in it," says Detective Andrew Houghton - and now podcast co-host - at Elgin Police Department in Illinois. He worked on Elgin's 2025 podcast Somebody Knows Something alongside Detective Matthew Vartarian with assistance from a local radio station. Houghton and Vartarian had just been assigned to Elgin's new cold case unit in 2024 when the chief informed them that the job would also involve podcasting. "We're already starting this new unit," Houghton recalls. "Why are we adding something else new on top of that?" Houghton and his partner begrudgingly began figuring out how to arrange episodes and soon discovered the process was also helping them structure the investigation. They formed different theories about what had happened to the missing 23-year-old, and each theory naturally formed an episode. The podcast not only generated tips but also gave the detectives more ways to find leads. They started going through posts on social media about their own programme. "They'd say, like, 'Oh, my mom worked with this person, or I live in this neighbourhood and I remember this.'" The detectives ultimately solved the case through old-fashioned policework; one of their theories had been that Schepers had crashed her car and ended up in the river. They had found a 1999 local newspaper story claiming that police had searched salvage yards by helicopter as well as dragging the Fox River but there was no evidence the latter had happened. And they did not shy away from telling listeners this. So the department brought in a search company with the latest sonar technology as well as divers - and they found Schepers and her car at the bottom of the river in March 2025. Now they're on the third season of the podcast. They shook up the format for the second, focusing on homicides, but have returned to a missing persons case. Houghton acknowledges that "it is a lot of work - it takes a lot of time and effort". As other departments navigate those budgetary and resource issues, however, there's a consensus that podcasts as an investigative tool will be seen more frequently. If police departments can find the staffing to sustain it, podcasting could help in both recruitment and staff retention, says Janice Iwama, associate professor in American University's department of justice, law and criminology. It gives listeners the chance to learn more about what policing is really like, from the mouths of working officers. Generational change could also fuel the trend, says retired NYPD Detective Alcazar, because younger police officers will be more ready to embrace the opportunities presented by podcasts and social media. "That's their world," he says. "That's what they're most comfortable with."

item.title: Greyhounds bound for Australia as New Zealand racing ban takes effect
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y62pe9g3no?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Greyhounds bound for Australia as New Zealand racing ban takes effect - Published At least two chartered flights carrying up to 150 greyhounds are set to fly to Australia's eastern states, as a New Zealand ban on the sport comes into effect. Several greyhound trainers in New Zealand are responding to a new ban by moving their dogs to Australia with plans to continue in the sport, governing body Greyhound Racing New Zealand (GRNZ) told the BBC. While the ban across New Zealand takes effect on Saturday, the practice remains legal almost everywhere in Australia. The ban was first announced in December 2024, and legislated in April. Approximately 1,400 greyhounds will retire in New Zealand under the ban and require rehoming. Australian authorities say that greyhounds arriving from New Zealand are classed as "companion animals" which will undergo screening for diseases such as rabies. "Australia's import requirements for dogs are based on biosecurity risk, not the intended use of the animal," Australia's Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry told a Senate inquiry in June. A spokesperson for New Zealand's Racing Minister Winston Peters called the plans to relocate the dogs "the last gasp actions of a dying industry". Peters said the dog racing industry had "lost its social licence" after multiple reviews concluded that dog and injury death rates "remain unacceptably high", a conclusion that GRNZ disputed. In a statement, a spokesperson for Peters said: "We understand a small number of dogs are being exported to Australia, but the vast majority (1,300 to 1,400) will be rehomed over the next couple of years." "This is a one-off final act rather than an ongoing issue," the spokesperson added. GRNZ Edward Rennell chief executive told the BBC that between six and 10 trainers have expressed interest in relocating to Australia, with most New Zealand citizens not requiring a special visa to live in Australia. Details would be finalised "over the next two weeks", he said. Rennell said "the details aren't locked in" but that his organisation would cover the full cost of the flights, while other costs would be borne by owners and trainers. "We will be supporting people that are looking to transfer over," Rennell said. He said some of the dogs will continue training and racing in Australia, although he noted they are likely to be less competitive in professional racing because breeding has largely paused in New Zealand since the ban was announced 18 months ago. Kiwis are still able to bet on Australian greyhound racing, which has a larger commercial presence. Queensland, New South Wales (NSW) and Victoria's industries were collectively worth almost A$2bn (£1.04bn; $1.4m) in 2022-23, which dwarfed New Zealand's $147m total, according to the latest figures published by Greyhounds Australasia. The dedicated body overseeing the closure of the industry in New Zealand, the Greyhound Transition Agency told the BBC: "We understand that arrangements are being made to relocate some dogs to Australia for racing purposes. "However, we are not in a position to comment further on these arrangements." New Zealand announced the greyhound racing ban following three independent reviews into the sport in 2013, 2017 and 2021. "We acknowledge the industry made advances in safety, but the high injury and death rates persisted with no sign of improvement," Peters's spokesperson added. In response, Rennell told the BBC: "I will go to my grave saying that the greyhound welfare standards are the best of any racing code in New Zealand." GRNZ has eyed kennels across eastern Australia as destinations for New Zealand's racing dogs. A spokesperson for the Queensland Racing Integrity Commission said the agency "has been advised by Greyhound Racing New Zealand of the arrival of racing greyhounds and the potential relocation of industry participants from New Zealand into Queensland". NSW and Victorian officials said they were not aware of specific relocation plans within their states, noting that greyhounds are permitted to travel across jurisdictions in Australia in New Zealand. Australia's Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry did not respond to a request to make further comment. Dozens of greyhounds were also found to have been moved to Australia after New Zealand's ban was first announced. Officials have confirmed 80 greyhounds were exported from New Zealand to Queensland through a chartered flight in April 2025. One trainer and his family were drawn to the "shining lights of the new facility" west of Brisbane, Simon Stout from Greyhounds Australasia told a parliamentary committee hearing in Tasmania on Wednesday. But one federal senator, Mehreen Faruqi of the Greens, told the BBC she was "deeply concerned about loopholes that allow the continued export of racing dogs to this country that neither New Zealand nor Australia seem to care about". Director of the Coalition for the Protection of Greyhounds Kylie Field said Australia already struggles to find residential homes for thousands of retired racing dogs, including 4,100 in NSW. "In an attempt to solve the rehoming crisis, the racing industry had devised a program of sending retired greyhounds to the US and Canada," Field said. "More than 2,000 dogs have been sent overseas so far." Dog racing is banned in the Australian Capital Territory and Tasmania has announced plans to phase it out. Scotland and Wales both passed legislation outlawing commercial dog racing this year. Most US states have imposed a ban, leaving two racing tracks in West Virginia as the last active operations. Watch: Tens of thousands of migrants enter Spain's Ceuta from Morocco About 60,000 migrants entered Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco on 30 July, with many swimming and using inflatables. Others ran through a gate in the border fence. Officials said almost all those who reached the enclave have returned, while Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said on Saturday that the death toll had risen to at least 67.
